subject: grace-reiter
research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-16, first run, mode create; the baseline was empty and there were no research notes or prior evidence). Leads: the backlog queue note (SNL Season 52 featured player; hometown conflict Madison vs Chippewa Falls; the podcast as main first-person record; Rolling Stone creators list). Opened about 20 web sources and the full podcast feed. Transcribed and read in full 38 long-form recordings (about 30 hours, roughly 350,000 words): 35 YouTube auto-caption transcripts (all 2025-2026 That's Enough episodes available, plus guest appearances on The Downside x2, Couch Surfing, Volley for Serve x2, Literally Life Changing, The Yvette Show, Business Casual Comedy, Wild Wild Web, Page Six, Kyle MacLachlan, I Never Liked You, The Comment Section), Whisper transcriptions of the Hunger Games making-of and two Passion Pod interviews (June 2022, December 2024). Readers extracted timestamped items; every quotation used in claims was rechecked against the transcript text. Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen.

Outcome: status ready, profile_format standard, leading read Type 6 at medium confidence, Type 3 the strongest alternative; Types 1, 9, 2, 7 and 4 tested and set aside (see type_hypothesis). Open-case format considered and rejected: her TikTok breakout dates to 2019-2020 and the first-person record is deep (four years, 30+ hours, plus testimony from her father, sister, roommate, producer and collaborators), so this is a hard typing, not a young record. Risks: contested_typing (Type 6 vs Type 3 is close and the record is comic) and sensitive_allegations (see the sensitivity task); the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-16). SNL Season 52 began September 26, 2026; she has appeared in each of the first three episodes (C13). SNL was not allowing her to give interviews as of September 17 and no post-casting interview was found (C13). Minimum Wage premieres on Netflix October 26, 2026 (C14). Twilight (but better) was shot in June 2026 and is not yet released (C15). The podcast has had no new episodes since May 11, 2026 (C08). Corrections to common sources: born in the Madison area, not Chippewa Falls (C01); podcast launched March 2025, not late 2024 (C08); full-time American High from 2023 (C07); never lived in LA long-term (C06); no ADHD diagnosis stated (C40); TIME100 Creators claim unverified (C38).

Drafting guidance. Lead with a concrete, sourced moment rather than the SNL announcement, for durability: for example the May 2025 overshare in which the comic famous for gross-out confessions chose as her "real" overshare that she feels "so guilty with the success I have" (C16), or her father's nickname "the shakes" for a girl who now performs live on SNL (C23). Make the argument through the praise-and-success pattern (C16-C19), then the vigilance and checking pattern (C20-C22), then how she steadies herself (C23, C25, C26, C34). Put Type 3 beside the main argument with its real evidence (C05, C30-C32) and say plainly what the discriminator is and where it is weak. Include the boldness and novelty she shows (C36, C37) and the bossy-older-sister material (C27) as complications, not footnotes. Use the SNL, Netflix and Twilight dates as context, not as the hook. Keep "## What is Grace Reiter's personality type?" with an answer of at most 60 words that says Type 6 is the leading read, with Type 3 the closest alternative. Do not claim a wing or subtype; none is defensible. Set enneagram: 6 and published: false.

Sensitivity. (a) Sexuality and romance: across episodes she describes her orientation and romantic history as uncertain and personal, mostly in jokes; do not state or imply an orientation, relationship status or sexual history, and do not use the refused-kiss story beyond, at most, her own short line (C24). (b) Health: no diagnosis (C40); her therapy (C28) may be mentioned only as she framed it publicly, briefly; body-image remarks recur and must not be used as evidence. (c) Substances: a first-weed-experience story and joke references to paranoia or "schizophrenia" are comic and must not be presented as health disclosures. (d) A story about selling non-explicit novelty videos to a fan who then sent an explicit message (The Downside, January 2025) involves a private person; omit. (e) Third-party allegations inside her stories (a high-school classmate described as abusive to a girlfriend; a cousin's criminal charge) concern private people; never repeat them. (f) Family: her mother wants privacy (S32); her grandmother's dementia (S39) and the family dog's death are private; her parents may be named once. (g) Molly's own anxiety and health disclosures in S32 are hers, not Grace's.

Quotation cautions. All transcripts are YouTube auto-captions without speaker names or Whisper transcriptions without speaker labels; check every printed quotation against the audio at the timestamp and remove only clear stutters. Known traps: the "becoming a Christian" overshare is Grace's (verified by context), even though a Stapleview clip of the same conversation is easily misread as the guest's; the ADHD and Adderall lines in S27 are Gianmarco Soresi's; the full-frontal story in S33 is the host's; the "shy older sister", King George III and NFL stories in S47 are Drew Afualo's; in the Passion Pod episodes "control freak" and metrics anxiety are the host's; Whisper renders "Hunger Games" as "Hongka Games" at the start of S31. Censored words appear as "[ __ ]"; quote them with the original bracket or a clearly marked substitution, not a guessed spelling. The January 6 answer in S40 and the dinosaur body-standards premise in S45 are bits. Cite the syndicated NYT copy (S09) that was read, not the unopened original (S49).

Follow-up for the next refresh: (1) transcribe the Eve Hartley interview about Twilight (but better) (S50) and any release-week interviews once Twilight is posted; (2) look for her first post-casting long-form interview, especially how she describes SNL's pressure, feedback and whether she feels she belongs; (3) after October 26, 2026, check Minimum Wage credits and reception; (4) transcribe That's Enough episodes that were not available as YouTube transcripts (Eps 2, 5, 6, 9-13, 19, 21, 27, 28, 31, 33, 36, 39, 44 and the remaining feed-only episodes, IP-blocked on 2026-10-16), the Gaydar episode, the Spooners short and the 2021 Drew Barrymore Show segment; (5) seek testimony from American High (Will Phelps, the Micho brothers, Julia DiCesare) or SNL colleagues; (6) confirm the Rolling Stone rank and whether a TIME100 Creators listing exists.

Draft log (2026-10-16, draft stage). Thesis: Type 6 at medium confidence; when approval arrives she pushes it away, wants an outside authority to hold it, and braces for a fall; Type 3 argued in its own section, Types 1, 9 and 2 after it, then a section on what the type does not explain (novelty, defiance, bossiness, trust, selective oversharing). Quote fidelity: all 122 quoted strings in the body were machine-matched (normalized) against the research stage's saved texts in /tmp/grace-reiter-research (vtt/ auto-captions and Whisper transcripts, txt/ print sources), and the thesis passages were reread in context by timestamp. Two quotes that crossed a host interjection or a caption repetition were split (S46 Ginger Twinsies; S47 "grimacing"). Not done at this stage: a second transcription from audio. The research log asked for audio checks of caption quotes; the edit or verify stage should audio-check at least S23 0:09:04-0:10:45, S42 0:08:12-0:08:47, S38 0:16:32 and 0:51:10, S39 0:41:20 and S47 1:28:05. S18, S19 and S31 are single Whisper transcriptions without speaker labels. Correction: C23 now follows the full S20 passage. The "the shakes" nickname followed a seventh-grade Hubble telescope speech; the eighth-grade choir solo came after (C91). Claims removed because the draft does not use them: C04 (high-school theater dispute; note S44, where she agrees she did no plays because of stage fright, also conflicts with S29), C32 ("I don't exist unless I mean funny", "shell"), C38 (Rolling Stone list), C40 (no diagnosis; the draft makes no health claim). Their sources are retained, and type_hypothesis text references to C32 were repointed to S25 and S40. Not printed by choice: the narcissist line (S20, medium attribution), the "attack mode" reply (S42, joke), the "rule followery" and "follow the rules" turns (S33, shared with the host), the "have I given you a complex" question (S37, medium attribution), the S47 "I just want to make a movie with my friends" line (not re-located at the cited timestamp), the refused-kiss story (S40), body-image context of S46, and all censored-word quotations. Added: S51 (RUSSH, opened from the saved copy) for the birth date; new claims C41-C116 map every quotation and metadata fact in draft.md. Interpretation claims are labeled as such. The quoted H2 headings repeat lines mapped in C17, C19, C23 and C68. Embed: S23 at 8:48-10:52. Internal links go to published pages only (tim-robinson, jennifer-lawrence and the Type 1/2/3/6/9 pages). birth_place is omitted because the record does not settle the city (Madison vs Verona). date and lastmod are the run date (empty baseline); published: false. No inherited production_pretext blockers (empty baseline).

sources.locator: Section "She's the first SNL cast member born after 2000".
sources.excerpt: Yep, Reiter was actually born May 18, 2001 – which also makes her a Taurus.
sources.context: Explainer published the day after the casting announcement. Read at the draft stage from the copy the research stage saved (raw/russh.html, txt/russh.txt). Secondary and probably not independent of Wikipedia (S06) for the date.

claims.claim: Introducing her May 2025 overshare, she said she would set aside her usual gross-out confessions.
claims.passage: she would "steer away from gross ones cuz I've been doing gross all the time."
claims.inference: S23 0:08:56-0:08:59: "I'm going to steer away from gross ones cuz I've been doing gross all the time." It frames the guilt confession as a deliberate departure from her usual material.
claims.alternative: Choosing a different kind of overshare is also a host varying her segment.

claims.claim: Her May 2025 "overshare" on her own podcast was guilt about success: "I feel so guilty with the success I have. I'm thinking about becoming a Christian."
claims.passage: "I feel so guilty with the success I have. I'm thinking about becoming a Christian."
claims.inference: She sets aside her usual gross-out overshares to offer this as the real one, and seven months later her roommate refers back to it unprompted ("why you wanted to find God", S42), so it reflects something persistent, not a one-off bit. It shows praise experienced as a weight she wants an outside authority to carry.
claims.alternative: Delivered with laughter and a riff on celebrity conversions; partly comic. Midwestern modesty and a young person's surprise at fast success are plausible circumstantial explanations. A Type 3 concerned with not appearing vain could say the first sentence, but the wish for an external authority to "give all of it" to fits Type 6 better. She later said she simply stopped thinking about the religion idea (S42).

claims.claim: She explained that frequent compliments overwhelm her and that believing in God would let her hand the praise to God.
claims.passage: Her guest, the comedian Veronika Slowikowska, laughed. Reiter explained that "people compliment me like a lot," and when they tell her "you're going to be something, kid," her reaction is "I can't handle this." Then: "But if I believed in God, I could give all of it to God." If you think she's awesome, she reasoned, "you think God's awesome."
claims.inference: S23 0:09:29-0:10:04, read in context: Veronika's laughter and "I resonate" come first; then Grace: "people compliment me like a lot and they're like, 'Oh, you're so like you're going to be something, kid.' ... And I'm like, 'I can't handle this.' And I'm like, 'But if I believed in God, I could give all of it to God.'" and "Like if you think I'm awesome, you think God's awesome." Praise is experienced as a weight to be carried by an outside authority.
claims.alternative: Delivered with laughter and followed by a riff on celebrity conversions (Bieber, Selena Gomez, Chance the Rapper); partly comic. Midwestern modesty or surprise at fast success could produce the same words.

claims.claim: In the same overshare she said she was terrified of her ego growing too large.
claims.passage: The delivery was comic, with a riff on celebrity converts. The worry underneath was stated plainly: "the ego can get so so large. And that's what I'm terrified of."
claims.inference: S23 0:10:41-0:10:45: "cuz the ego can get so so large. And that's what I'm terrified of." The fear attaches to success, not failure.
claims.alternative: A Type 3 worried about looking vain could say this; the sentence alone does not discriminate.

claims.claim: Grace Marie Reiter was born on May 18, 2001, in the Madison area of Wisconsin and grew up in Chippewa Falls, where her family moved in 2007; she graduated from Chippewa Falls High School in 2019 and has posted sketch comedy online since 2019.
claims.passage: Reiter, born in 2001 near Madison, Wisconsin, and raised in Chippewa Falls, has posted sketch comedy online since 2019.
claims.inference: Her father (via the Leader-Telegram) says the family lived in Madison, where she was born, and moved back in 2007. Wikipedia gives the full date and cites a Capital Times St. Mary's Hospital birth notice and Chippewa Herald birthday notices (not opened). In 2022 she said she was "born in Verona, just a little south of Madison" and moved back "like in first grade". Safe wording: born in the Madison area (or "near Madison"), raised in Chippewa Falls.
claims.alternative: Milwaukee Magazine says "born and raised in Chippewa Falls" and trade outlets say "originally from Chippewa Falls"; those are wrong or loose on birthplace. Verona versus a Madison hospital is unresolved; do not print a city of birth more precise than the Madison area. The full date rests on Wikipedia's cited notices plus Russh; it is consistent with her age (25 in September 2026).

claims.claim: She was an original cast member of Stapleview, a live TikTok sketch show created by former Broadway Video producer Sam Grey that premiered March 3, 2022 and was filmed in Los Angeles; she then lived in a short-term sublet in LA, not a permanent move.
claims.passage: In 2022 she was an original cast member of _Stapleview_, a live TikTok sketch show
claims.inference: Contemporaneous reporting. In 2022 and 2024 she describes the LA stint as about three months and says she never moved there.
claims.alternative: The Leader-Telegram says she "moved to Burbank, Calif." after graduating; that most likely describes the Stapleview stint. Avoid saying she lived in LA long-term.

claims.claim: American High, a Syracuse-area film company, recruited her as a guest around February 2023 and hired her full-time around July 2023 as one of five core cast members of American High Shorts and College Life, relocating her to Syracuse; by fall 2024 she was no longer part of the shorts, and she moved to New York City in December 2024. She did not attend Syracuse University.
claims.passage: from 2023 she worked in Syracuse as one of five core cast members of American High's sketch shorts.
claims.inference: Her own consistent dating ("July of 2023 to October 2024", S33; guest about February 2023 and full-time about July 2023, S19) plus contemporaneous Daily Orange and Panther reporting. NYC move from S20 (arrived about December 9, 2024) and S30.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia and CNY Central say she joined in late 2022 (Phelps began trialing comedians in October 2022). She still appears in Minimum Wage, an American High production. Use "2023" or "from 2023" for the full-time role.

claims.claim: She appeared on HBO's The Chair Company, which premiered in October 2025.
claims.passage: In October 2025 she appeared on HBO's _The Chair Company_.
claims.inference: NYT (S09): she plays Tara on the show, which "wrapped up its first season in November"; Wikipedia (S06) lists a recurring role in six episodes. The draft prints only the appearance and month.
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: She posted "The Hunger Games (but better)," a nearly 45-minute parody she directed and starred in as Katniss, on YouTube on November 19, 2025.
claims.passage: A month later she posted _The Hunger Games (but better)_, a nearly 45-minute parody she directed and starred in.
claims.inference: Release date and views from her channel and press; motive line is her own narration (S31, check audio because Whisper misheard the title).
claims.alternative: View counts are time-sensitive; write "more than 13 million views by September 2026". She also frames the project as a gift to her friends and says the idea came from improvising with friends (C34), so "she wanted to be the lead" should not stand alone.

claims.claim: NBC named her a featured player on SNL in September 2026; at 25 she is the first SNL cast member born in the 21st century.
claims.passage: In September 2026 NBC named her a featured player on _Saturday Night Live_. At 25, [The New York Times](https://www.boston.com/culture/entertainment/2026/09/18/snl-new-cast-2026/) noted, she was the show's first cast member born in the 21st century.
claims.inference: Deadline (S07) announced the hire on September 16, 2026; the NYT syndicated text (S09) says "At 25, she is the first 'SNL' cast member born in the 21st century."
claims.alternative: Featured-player status changes at season end.
claims.review_trigger: Revisit at the end of Season 52 (about May 2027): renewal, promotion to repertory or departure.

claims.claim: Her father says SNL was her long-held goal.
claims.passage: that SNL had "been her goal forever."
claims.inference: Leader-Telegram (S05): "'It's been her goal forever. It's completely surreal.'" said of the SNL casting.
claims.alternative: A proud parent speaking on the day of the announcement.

claims.claim: The article draws on about four years of her own interviews and podcast episodes plus testimony from people who live and work with her.
claims.passage: This analysis follows what she does when the goal starts arriving, across about four years of her interviews and podcast episodes and the testimony of people who live and work with her.
claims.inference: First-person record runs from Passion Pod (S18, recorded about May 2022) to The Comment Section (S47, September 2026); testimony comes from her roommate (S42), producer (S41), father (S05), sister (S32) and collaborators (S39, S45).
claims.alternative: The record is mostly comic podcasting; see type_hypothesis limits.

claims.claim: Type 6 thesis: her fear shows up when things go well; she pushes praise away, wants someone or something to hold her success, and expects it to be taken from her.
claims.passage: Grace Reiter's personality type is Enneagram Type 6, the Loyalist. Sixes sit in the head triad, whose core emotion is fear. Reiter's fear shows up when things go well: she pushes praise away, wishes for someone or something to hold her success, and expects it to be taken from her.
claims.inference: Summarizes C16-C19 and C61: praise deflected (S42, S39, S30), success handed to God (S23), downfall predicted after a hit (S38). Interpretation at medium confidence, stated in the next paragraphs.
claims.alternative: Type 3 reads the same deflection as image management (see type_hypothesis.alternative_case).

claims.claim: Much of her vigilance is aimed at her own rise and the ego she fears.
claims.passage: Reiter aims much of it at her own rise: the praise, the views, the ego she is "terrified of."
claims.inference: Draws on "the ego can get so so large. And that's what I'm terrified of" (S23) and the post-hit downfall line (S38).
claims.alternative: Fear of ego can also be ordinary modesty.

claims.claim: The type read is medium-confidence, with Type 3 the main rival.
claims.passage: The read is medium-confidence.
claims.inference: Mirrors type_hypothesis.confidence and alternative_type.
claims.alternative: See type_hypothesis.against.

claims.claim: When her roommate began to praise her on her podcast, she cut him off.
claims.passage: He began to praise her, and she cut him off: "we can't do this on my podcast."
claims.inference: S42 0:08:12-0:08:18: Max: "I think you are a singular" / Grace: "Oh god. Okay. We can't No, we can't do this on my podcast." Episode released April 6, 2026; recorded after the parody's release (Max mentions people calling her Katniss).
claims.alternative: Playful; she then jokes about being shouted out in an award speech.

claims.claim: Her roommate Max Zavidow says she hates compliments more than anyone he knows.
claims.passage: "Well, what's funny is that you hate compliments more than anyone I know."
claims.inference: Testimony from someone with daily access (S42 0:08:27). With C64, C79 and C68 it is the core of the discriminator against Type 3: approval is deflected rather than taken in.
claims.alternative: Comic self-deprecation is a technique she names ("comedy 101", S27), and deflecting compliments is a Midwestern norm. She answers that she is getting better at it (C66). Her "attack mode" reply in the same exchange is joke-framed and is not printed.

claims.claim: Her roommate linked her dislike of compliments to the earlier wish to find God.
claims.passage: He tied it, unprompted, to the overshare from months before: "It's the same thing of like why you wanted to find God."
claims.inference: S42 0:08:35-0:08:44: "It's the same thing of like why you wanted to find God because you were like ... people are like too nice about it." Shows the May 2025 overshare reflected something persistent.
claims.alternative: He may know the overshare from the published episode rather than from home life.

claims.claim: She protested that she is good at taking compliments now; he allowed she was getting better.
claims.passage: She protested, "No, I feel like I'm good at it now." "Okay, you're getting better," he allowed.
claims.alternative: Shows change over time; the aversion may be easing.

claims.claim: Strangers now call her Katniss, which she says was kind of always her dream.
claims.passage: Strangers on the street now shout [Jennifer Lawrence](/personality-analysis/jennifer-lawrence)'s name at her and call her Katniss, she said, "which I guess was kind of always my dream."
claims.inference: S42 0:08:48-0:08:56: "I walked on the street, people go Jennifer Lawrence, Hunger Games. Yeah, people are like they call me Katniss now, which I guess was kind of always my dream." Counterweight: she enjoys the recognition.
claims.alternative: Supports the Type 3 reading as much as Type 6.

claims.claim: Asked months after the overshare whether she still felt called to Christianity, she said no and that she simply doesn't think about it now.
claims.passage: Later in the episode he asked whether she still felt called to Christianity. She said no. "I think I just like don't think about it," she said. "I think I'm just like, okay, well, this is my life and this is the things I want to do."
claims.inference: S42 0:45:47-0:46:12: "have you been feeling that more recently?" / "No." / "I just I think I just like don't think about it. I think I'm just like, okay, well, this is my life and this is the things I want to do. So, like this stuff is going to happen." Counterevidence kept in the article: the guilt may be easing as she adjusts to success.
claims.alternative: Could equally show a Six settling into a situation once it feels familiar.

claims.claim: Gianmarco Soresi says she underplayed the parody before its premiere; when he praised her directing she credited the source film.
claims.passage: that before the premiere "you were really underplaying it," and praised her directing. She credited the source film ("it also like again already did exist"), then said:
claims.inference: S39 0:40:17-0:41:20: Soresi: "you were really underplaying it" before he saw it at the premiere; then praise of her directing; Grace: "Well, it also like again already did exist."
claims.alternative: Comedians routinely minimize their own projects; three voices with sparse speaker markers, but these turns are pinned by content.

claims.claim: She answered Soresi's compliment with an apology.
claims.passage: "But thank you for the compliment. Thank you for the compliment. I'm sorry."
claims.inference: S39 0:41:20-0:41:23, the line immediately after C64.
claims.alternative: Possibly a comic beat; the apology is still an observed response to praise.

claims.claim: Told by Busy Philipps that she is "big in our house," she said she isn't allowed to perceive herself that way: "that's not for me" and "Like I'm for you guys."
claims.passage: When the actor Busy Philipps told her on [_That's Enough_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kR3EE_G-EY4) in November 2025 that she was "big in our house," where Philipps's daughters are fans, Reiter objected: "I don't think you're allowed to perceive yourself like that, though. You can't." Asked why, she said, "that's not for me," and then, "Like I'm for you guys."
claims.inference: S30 0:40:40-0:40:52 (November 3, 2025). A deliberate refusal to own popularity.
claims.alternative: A healthy, borrowed philosophy of craft could explain it; it is also what a Type 3 trying not to be ruled by metrics might adopt.

claims.claim: She cited Madonna on being the manager of one's talent and said not owning the talent keeps her from tying self-worth to views and likes.
claims.passage: She had just watched a clip of Madonna describing the artist as "the manager of your talent." The idea "makes me feel good," she said, because she isn't "the owner of it." Otherwise "you start tying your selfworth to all of it and then it gets you know like the views and the likes."
claims.inference: S30 0:42:22-0:43:05. Note on order: "that makes me feel good because I'm like I'm not um like the owner of it" comes just before the Madonna sentence in the source; the article's "The idea" refers to the shared idea that the talent is not hers.
claims.alternative: She calls this passage "kind of my overshare"; could be borrowed wisdom rather than anxiety.

claims.claim: Of The Chair Company she said people told her she did well, that she didn't think she was acting at all, and "oh my god, I tricked them all."
claims.passage: Of _The Chair Company_, created by and starring [Tim Robinson](/personality-analysis/tim-robinson), she told the actor Kyle MacLachlan [in April 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMtFoCeII34) that "people have told me I did good in the show." "I don't think I was acting at all," she said, and then, "oh my god, I tricked them all."
claims.inference: S44 0:18:54-0:19:07 (April 22, 2026). Praise answered with an impostor joke.
claims.alternative: Impostor feelings are common in a first big job; MacLachlan reframes it as being in the moment.

claims.claim: She barely talked to Tim Robinson on set because she was scared and intimidated.
claims.passage: she barely talked to Robinson "cuz I was scared. I was intimidated."
claims.inference: S33 0:48:46-0:48:50 (December 3, 2025): "I didn't really also talk to him a lot cuz I was scared. I was intimidated."
claims.alternative: A newcomer around a show's creator; ordinary.

claims.claim: Self-mockery is her stated comic method, and compliment-deflection is ordinary Midwestern politeness.
claims.passage: She has called self-mockery "comedy 101," and she grew up in the Upper Midwest, where waving off a compliment is ordinary politeness.
claims.inference: S27 0:28:35 "Isn't that like comedy 101? Like just [ __ ] on yourself". The Midwest point is an author observation; she names her Midwest identity in S33 ("Midwest freaking represent").
claims.alternative: This is the circumstance alternative to the type reading.

claims.claim: She wants attention on her birthday but does not want to ask for it.
claims.passage: "I want the attention but I also don't want to ask for it."
claims.inference: S41 0:02:15-0:02:19; episode recorded February 18, 2026, released March 30, 2026. Shows the aversion is to direct praise, not to attention.
claims.alternative: Common feeling about birthdays.

claims.claim: In February 2026 she said that episode was the only time she felt she had truly overshared.
claims.passage: "This actually this has been the only time in the podcast where I've actually felt like I have overshared," she said.
claims.inference: S38 0:50:58-0:51:04. The story itself (sensitive) is not described.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: After the parody's success she predicted, half-jokingly, that her own hand would bring her down.
claims.passage: "I knew this was going to happen too because The Hunger Games was so successful. I was like something's going to happen and it is my own hand that brings down myself."
claims.inference: S38 0:51:10-0:51:17 (episode released February 9, 2026). Anticipating danger at the moment of success is a Type 6 signature; a Type 3 more typically fears failure and being seen failing.
claims.alternative: A half-joke about an embarrassing overshare in that episode, not about her career. The January 2025 "biggest fear is that I'm a narcissist" line (S20, medium attribution) is not printed. Treat as supporting, not decisive.

claims.claim: The downfall line is half a joke but shows a habit of looking for the fall at the moment of success.
claims.passage: It was half a joke, about an embarrassing story rather than a career. But it describes a habit: at the moment of success, she looks for the fall.
claims.inference: Pattern across S23 (ego fear), S22 (fear of success) and S38.
claims.alternative: One half-joke cannot establish a habit by itself; the claim rests on the other two sources.

claims.claim: Asked how she keeps success from becoming a fear of failure, she said it is less a fear of failure than a fear of actually trying.
claims.passage: In April 2025 the creator Coy Piso asked her on his show, [_Couch Surfing_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0bP_zcZydbs), how she kept the possibility of success from turning into a fear of failure. "I don't know if it's necessarily a fear of failure," she said. It was "maybe like a fear of actually trying."
claims.inference: S22 1:04:40-1:05:15, recorded April 20, 2025; Coy wrote the question himself. Two-person conversation, high attribution.
claims.alternative: She hedges in the same answer ("which I mean I guess maybe it kind of is").

claims.claim: She describes a lifelong habit of half-effort: "my whole life I've kind of half halfass everything" (April 2025).
claims.passage: "I feel like my whole life I've kind of half halfass everything."
claims.inference: S22 1:05:22-1:05:25, printed as captioned ("half halfass" is the auto-caption rendering). Fear of full effort fits Type 6 (and Type 9) better than Type 3 or Type 1.
claims.alternative: Her output contradicts the label (weekly podcast, self-produced parody, nightly open mics); the laziness may be self-image, not behavior. Audio not re-checked at this stage.

claims.claim: Now that success is arriving, she says, the fear is of success being even bigger than she imagined.
claims.passage: Now that she was "starting to see the success that I wanted," she said, "the fear is actually being successful like the possibility of like oh this could be even bigger than I thought it could be."
claims.alternative: Could be ordinary nerves about a growing career.

claims.claim: In 2022 she called not taking herself seriously her recurring mistake and said Los Angeles taught her maybe she was not an awful person.
claims.passage: In 2022, living back in Wisconsin after a few months in Los Angeles with _Stapleview_, she told the local [_Passion Pod_](https://downloads.pod.co/dd47e031-3896-47f1-8ac5-ce83f089122f/b5816dc0-61ed-41ac-8eca-e06d4e86e438.mp3) that her recurring mistake was "not taking myself more seriously like allowing myself to say I'm a comedian or allowing myself to say I'm an actress." The trip had taught her "maybe I'm not an awful horrible person."
claims.inference: S18 00:55:26-00:55:49 (Whisper transcript, no speaker labels; she is answering the host's question). Recorded about May 2022 while she lived with her parents after Stapleview.
claims.alternative: Common self-doubt at 20 or 21; Whisper text not checked against a second transcription.

claims.claim: Interpretation: for a Six, success raises the stakes; her words fit that better than fear of failing.
claims.passage: For a Six, success can raise the stakes: more to lose, more people watching, more ways to be found out. Her words fit that better than they fit a fear of failing.
claims.inference: Built on C84, C85, C19, C62.
claims.alternative: Circumstance (next sentence) explains part of it.

claims.claim: Her career moved from TikTok to HBO, Netflix and SNL in about a year, an ordinary cause of impostor feelings.
claims.passage: In about a year her career moved from TikTok to HBO, Netflix and SNL, which would give anyone in her mid-20s reasons to feel like an impostor.
claims.inference: The Chair Company (October 2025), the Netflix order (April 2026) and the SNL hire (September 2026); she says "maybe it is imposter syndrome" (S22).
claims.alternative: This is the circumstantial alternative stated in the article.

claims.claim: On her oversharing show she says everything she overshares makes her ask, "Is that okay?"
claims.passage: "Why did I make this whole podcast over sharing when everything I over share I'm like, 'Is that okay?'"
claims.inference: S38 0:16:34-0:16:40 (episode released February 9, 2026). Permission-checking on her own show.
claims.alternative: Followed by "I guess that's the point of it"; partly self-mocking.

claims.claim: After an embarrassing night she asked her friends whether they thought of her differently; they said they didn't care.
claims.passage: "Do you guys think of me differently now?" They told her they didn't care.
claims.inference: S33 1:26:10-1:26:13 (December 3, 2025). The night's details (a first-weed story with joke references) are not printed per the sensitivity task.
claims.alternative: Ordinary embarrassment.

claims.claim: She says she hopes her friends are actually her friends.
claims.passage: "I just like hope my friends are actually my friends."
claims.alternative: Max calls it a normal fear; joke-adjacent context about being high.

claims.claim: She expected the parody's commenters to be mean to her, and they weren't.
claims.passage: "I'm always like someone they're going to be mean to me and they never are, which is very sweet."
claims.inference: S46 0:16:47-0:16:51 (recorded summer 2026). The specific expected comments concerned her body; that context is deliberately not printed (sensitivity task b).
claims.alternative: Fear of comment-section cruelty is near-universal for creators.

claims.claim: She avoids opinion shows because she does not want to be judged for her opinions.
claims.passage: On opinion shows such as _Subway Takes_, which she has avoided "because I don't have an opinion and I don't want to be judged for my opinion."
claims.inference: S45 0:35:44-0:35:49 (May 11, 2026), introducing a satirical hot take on the same episode.
claims.alternative: Said while setting up a bit; medium sincerity.

claims.claim: Her roommate calls her one of the all-time great haters; she says she holds back because she is afraid of offending people and it could come back to her, and calls herself a people pleaser.
claims.passage: Her sharper opinions mostly stay private. Zavidow calls her "one of the all-time great haters." Her explanation: "I think it's because I'm afraid of like offending people." She holds back, she said, because "maybe it could come back to me." In September 2025 she told Soresi, on [her own show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PmHpEfGp0yY), "I think I'm a people pleaser."
claims.inference: S42 0:22:06-0:22:28 ("maybe it could come back to me" ends before a ">>" marker; the following words are not quoted); S27 0:26:29. Restraint explained by anticipated consequences fits Type 6 (and Types 1, 2, 9).
claims.alternative: Type 2 people-pleasing aims at being liked and needed; nothing in the record shows her seeking to be needed (she says "please text me cuz like I won't text you", C29). Type 9 conflict-avoidance would not usually coexist with this much private sharpness.

claims.claim: She avoided raising a complaint with an American High roommate, then blurted it at breakfast in front of everyone because she was so nervous.
claims.passage: When she does confront someone, it comes out sideways. At American High, she told Yvette, a roommate kept leaving paper towels around. She said nothing, then raised it "at like the worst time ever," at breakfast in front of everyone, with a guest star in the house. She said "it like felt like it spilled out of me because I was so nervous to tell him." He asked why she hadn't just told him before. Her verdict: "sometimes it's just that easy, but you build it up in your head."
claims.inference: S33 1:06:13-1:07:09. The roommate is a private person and is not named. Her causal reading is printed only up to "you build it up in your head"; the words after a ">>" marker are not quoted.
claims.alternative: Single source for the story; conflict-avoidance is shared by Types 2, 6 and 9. It sits beside self-described bluntness ("I'm very like blunt or like curt", S36), which is the counterphobic side of the same pattern or simply Midwestern directness.

claims.claim: The Micho brothers describe her hedging when invited and walking back her own questions when not answered at once.
claims.passage: Her longtime collaborators, the brothers Ryan and Aidan Micho, see the same reflex. When they asked whether she was coming on their podcast, one of them recalled in May 2026, she answered, "Do you want me to only if you want me to?" Later in that episode one of them told her, "If we don't answer within like the first 0.1 seconds, you immediately get shy and walk it down."
claims.inference: S45 0:07:27-0:07:33 (a host recounts her reply "Do you want me to only if you want me to?"; she adds "I don't want to like intrude") and 0:09:35-0:09:42 (a host: "If we don't answer within like the first 0.1 seconds, you immediately get shy and walk it down"). Which brother speaks is not labeled.
claims.alternative: Friendly ribbing between longtime collaborators; recounted, not observed by the author.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her checking follows the Six loop of scanning for disapproval and testing it against what people say.
claims.passage: This is the Six's checking loop: scan for hidden disapproval, then test it against what people actually say.
claims.inference: Built on C20, C70-C73.
claims.alternative: See next claim.

claims.claim: Fear of judgment is common for young performers with large followings, and she tells these stories as self-jokes.
claims.passage: Fear of judgment is also close to universal for a young performer with millions of followers and a comment section, and she tells most of these stories as jokes on herself.
claims.inference: Follower counts: 3.9 million TikTok (S05), about 4 million (S09).
claims.alternative: This is the alternative explanation, stated in the article.

claims.claim: She traces her stage fright to a seventh-grade class speech about the Hubble telescope, when her hands shook; after she told her father, he called her "the shakes," and from then on she believed she had stage fright.
claims.passage: Reiter dates her stage fright to middle school. In January 2025 she told Soresi on [_The Downside_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iE7kKL0kUAk) that running for class president in sixth grade hadn't scared her. Then, in seventh grade, during a speech about the Hubble telescope, her hands shook so badly she could barely flip her note cards. She told her father, "and then he called me the shakes." From then on, she said, she believed she had stage fright.
claims.inference: Corrected at draft from the full S20 passage (0:21:15-0:23:28, January 7, 2025): she was not scared running for class president in sixth grade; "seventh grade I gave a speech about the Hubble telescope ... I was shaking so bad ... I told my dad that and then he called me the shakes and then from then on out I was like oh I have stage fight [sic]". The research record tied the nickname to the eighth-grade choir solo; in her telling the choir solo (C91) came after.
claims.alternative: Stage fright is common and partly physiological. Grade numbers are her recollection.

claims.claim: She does not think her father understood how much the nickname would affect her.
claims.passage: "I don't think he understood how personally or how much that was going to affect me."
claims.inference: S20 0:23:20-0:23:28, answering whether her father was joking ("I hope so").
claims.alternative: Her father is described warmly elsewhere; this is not a complaint about his parenting.

claims.claim: In eighth grade she won a choir solo but, unable to sing it in front of a new pianist, hid behind the last row and cried; the solo was reassigned. She has retold the story at least three times.
claims.passage: She said she hoped he had been joking. The next year she won a choir solo in "You Raise Me Up," but in rehearsal she could not sing it in front of one new person, the pianist. She hid behind the last row and cried, and the solo went to someone else. "I was so mad at myself," she said. She has told the choir story at least three times, in January 2025, [July 2025](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YatrI4ziPjA) and April 2026.
claims.inference: S20 0:20:20-0:21:55 ("I literally like laid behind the last row and like hid", "I was so mad at myself"); S24 0:00:18-0:02:16 (July 7, 2025); S44 0:07:13-0:07:22 (April 22, 2026).
claims.alternative: In S44 she agrees she did not do plays in high school because of stage fright, while in S29 she says she played Elizabeth Proctor in The Crucible; the article makes no claim about high-school theater.

claims.claim: She now performs live on SNL.
claims.passage: The girl who could not sing in front of a pianist now performs live on network television.
claims.inference: Premiere recap (S10) and official October 2026 sketch uploads (S16).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Preparing for her 2024 SNL showcase left her "not even nervous at all."
claims.passage: "I like knew that that was coming. So I like worked for it and I practiced and then I was like, not even nervous at all."
claims.inference: S19 00:31:33-00:31:38 (Whisper, no speaker labels; she is answering the host's lesson question). Recorded about October-November 2024 in Wisconsin before the December 2024 move.
claims.alternative: Preparation is also how Type 3 and Type 1 manage performance.

claims.claim: She credited preparation over talent while saying she is good at it, and said she acts when someone else sets the obligation.
claims.passage: She credited the preparation over the talent: "it's not because I'm like good at this, which I think I am good at it, but I am good at it." And she has learned that she moves when "somebody else is like, hey, you have to do this."
claims.alternative: The assertion of skill is a counterweight to her self-deprecation.

claims.claim: Her 2024 SNL showcase did not lead to a hire; that December she called SNL "the dream" but doubted she could handle the work and preferred one-and-done projects; she went through the 2026 showcases and NBC announced her hire on September 16, 2026.
claims.passage: That showcase did not lead to a job. That December she said, "obviously SNL is like the dream," but "I don't know if I could handle that work," and she preferred "a one and done thing." In the summer of 2026 she went through the showcases again, and on September 16 NBC [announced](https://deadline.com/2026/09/snl-season-52-casts-grace-reiter-saidah-belo-osagie-1237105604/) her hire.
claims.inference: Her own 2024 account of the first showcase plus Deadline and NYT reporting of the 2026 hire. In 2024 she called SNL "the dream" but said "I don't know if I could handle that work" and preferred "one and done" projects.
claims.alternative: Her 2024 showcase outcome is inferred from the record (she never says she advanced, and she was not hired); do not claim she was "rejected" in stronger terms than that. Her father says SNL invited her to the 2026 showcase.
claims.review_trigger: Revisit at the end of Season 52 (about May 2027): contract renewal, promotion to repertory, or departure.

claims.claim: She dreads live comedy shows, stresses herself out, then has fun once on stage.
claims.passage: Dread before and fine after is her routine with live comedy too. "I stress myself out," she told Zavidow, and then "I get up there and I have fun and I'm like oh it's like fine."
claims.inference: S42 0:31:31-0:31:49, after Max describes the pre-show dread. Anticipatory anxiety followed by relief.
claims.alternative: Pre-show nerves are near-universal among comedians.

claims.claim: She wrote in her journal "I want a teacher. I want a mentor. I want a father," adding that she wrote the last part mostly because it sounded poetic; to Busy Philipps she said she wished her parents had punished her more.
claims.passage: She also looks for guidance outside herself. In her journal, she told Soresi in February 2026, she wrote, "I want a teacher. I want a mentor. I want a father." She added at once that she wrote the last one mostly because it sounded poetic, and she speaks of her father warmly. When Philipps wondered aloud whether she should be doing her own kids' homework, Reiter said of her parents, "If anything I wish they punished me more."
claims.inference: A wish for a trustworthy authority to lean on is a central Type 6 theme and ties to C16 (giving success "to God").
claims.alternative: She explicitly frames "I want a father" as poetic license, not a complaint about her own father, whom she describes warmly. Young artists commonly want mentors. The punishment line was partly said to reassure Busy Philipps, who had called herself a bad mom.

claims.claim: She described bringing her therapist a list of the day's mistakes; Soresi said her inner monologue sounds like a "completely non-functional human being" yet "you don't miss things."
claims.passage: In therapy, she told Soresi, she brought "a list of like all like the mistakes I made today." Hearing her describe her inner monologue, he said "you're a completely non-functional human being," then pointed out that she produces anyway: "you don't miss things."
claims.inference: S39 0:11:22-0:12:57 (February 24, 2026). Therapy summarized lightly, as she framed it publicly. The "worst person in the world" line is not printed.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest evidence for Type 1 (an inner critic reviewing mistakes). Against Type 1: her self-review asks whether she hurt or offended people rather than whether she did things correctly, she seeks others' reassurance rather than relying on an inner standard (C20), and she describes half-effort and mess tolerance a Type 1 would not accept (C25). Much of the sibling material is affectionate teasing; therapy content is sensitive and should be summarized lightly.

claims.claim: Interpretation: for a Six, safety comes from preparation, external obligations and trusted guides, which is where she finds her footing.
claims.passage: For a Six, safety comes from preparation, from obligations someone else sets and from trusted guides. That is where Reiter finds her footing.
claims.inference: Built on C92, C93, C26, C42.
claims.alternative: Preparation and mentors also suit Type 1 and Type 3.

claims.claim: Her ambition is old, explicit and measured in numbers.
claims.passage: The best case against the Six reading is her ambition, which is old, explicit and measured in numbers.
claims.inference: Introduces C05, C03, C30, C96.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: In 2022, at 20, she described her ambition in terms of online identity: "I grew up in the YouTube era. YouTubers were my celebrities. I think my dream had always been to be an Internet persona." She also said the persona carries pressure: "you have to be this persona and you don't want to overthink it ... Because that's what made people like you in the first place."
claims.passage: "I grew up in the YouTube era," she told [Volume One](https://volumeone.org/sites/chippewafalls/articles/2022/03/29/293816-from-chippewa-falls-to-la-grace-reiter-joins), a Chippewa Falls magazine, in March 2022. "YouTubers were my celebrities. I think my dream had always been to be an Internet persona." She described the pressure to stay that persona, "Because that's what made people like you in the first place."
claims.inference: Early evidence that being seen and liked online was the goal, and that she felt the liked self had to be maintained. The second quote expresses fear of losing what made people like her.
claims.alternative: Read as Type 3 (identity fused with an image that wins approval), this is the strongest early evidence for the alternative. Read as Type 6, it is worry about losing approval she cannot trust. A 20-year-old describing the creator economy accurately also explains it.

claims.claim: Her father says she has always been a ham for the camera who loved attention.
claims.passage: Her father says she has "always been a ham for the camera, and loved attention."
claims.inference: Independent of her own self-presentation and consistent with her account of making videos since middle school. It supports a long-held drive to perform; it does not by itself say what motive drives it.
claims.alternative: A proud parent speaking on the day of a career milestone; attention-loving in childhood is common and is not type-specific (Types 2, 3, 6 and 7 can all present this way).

claims.claim: Her follower goals keep moving: "I feel like the goalpost is always moving cuz once I hit 1 million, I was like, 'Yeah, but like all the really Tik Tok famous people have 3 million.'"
claims.passage: "I feel like the goalpost is always moving cuz once I hit 1 million, I was like, 'Yeah, but like all the really Tik Tok famous people have 3 million.'"
claims.inference: Repeated from April 2025 to August 2026. This is the core of the Type 3 alternative: metrics and recognition as yardsticks of worth, with escalating goals.
claims.alternative: For Type 6 the same ladder reads as an inability to feel arrived or safe ("It never feels real", "imposter syndrome", S22). She also says she avoids looking at numbers and wants to stop tying worth to "views and likes" (C18). In 2022 she withheld her analytics from her manager because her TikTok was underperforming (S18), which can be read as image protection (Type 3) or fear of judgment (Type 6).

claims.claim: Early in her fame she went to the Mall of America to be recognized, and she said she would be embarrassed if the parody got under a million views.
claims.passage: Early in her fame she went to the Mall of America "cuz there's going to be a lot of people there and I feel like I have to get recognized by someone." Of the parody she said, "If I don't get a million, I'm actually going to be really really embarrassed."
claims.inference: S22 0:57:16-0:57:33; the visit was early in her fame (Coy notes the photo is from December 2019, so her "post-COVID" framing was off; no date is printed). S46 0:12:01-0:12:07.
claims.alternative: Wanting to be recognized after going viral is common; both lines fit Type 3 and Type 6.

claims.claim: She made the parody because she wanted to be the lead in a movie for her birthday.
claims.passage: She made it, she said in the [making-of video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l52Dh0lQbIc), because "I want to be the lead in a movie for my birthday."
claims.inference: S31 00:00:39 (Whisper; her direct-to-camera narration).
claims.alternative: She also frames the shoot as a group project with friends (C34); the idea came from friends improvising.

claims.claim: She takes pride in casting the parody: "I casted everybody perfectly."
claims.passage: ("I casted everybody perfectly")
claims.inference: S32 0:12:47 (her sister was guest). Credit-taking counterweight to C34. Her spreadsheets and planning (S31, S34) are not printed.
claims.alternative: Planning fits several types: Type 6 (preparation as safety; she says practicing made her "not even nervous at all" before the 2024 SNL showcase, S19), Type 3 (efficient execution toward a goal) and Type 1 (getting it right). It does not discriminate on its own.

claims.claim: She says she does not take time to process or enjoy anything and is "work mode all the time" (August 2026).
claims.passage: and in August 2026 she said, "I don't take time to really process or enjoy anything. I'm just like work mode all the time."
claims.inference: A Type 3 pattern (doing over feeling) and also consistent with Type 6 restlessness and anxiety when idle.
claims.alternative: Her 2024 self-description was "floating... thing to thing" and "I'm having fun"; the 2026 lines come in her busiest year (Netflix series, Twilight, SNL audition), so circumstance explains part of it.

claims.claim: Told she makes every joke as hard as she can, she said she is always saying she could do more, be bigger, go harder, so it is good to know it is landing.
claims.passage: Told by the comedian Eric Sedeño [in January 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yjs2d3Yrwe4) that she makes every joke as hard as she can, she said, "I feel like I'm always saying I could do more, be bigger, go harder. So like it's good to know it's landing."
claims.inference: S36 0:15:14-0:15:36 (January 1, 2026). Supports the Type 3 reading; also a reassurance check.
claims.alternative: Both types fit.

claims.claim: Discriminator: a Three takes admiration in and converts it to the next goal; she pushes it away, and two people with close access describe the aversion independently.
claims.passage: So why does the Six lead? It comes down to what happens when the approval comes. A Three tends to take admiration in as proof and turn it into the next goal. Reiter pushes it away. She apologizes for a compliment, wants God to hold the praise, borrows Madonna's idea that she only manages her talent, and after her biggest hit predicts her own downfall. Her roommate and Soresi, who see her up close, describe the aversion independently, and in September 2026 a third host noticed it too.
claims.inference: Mirrors type_hypothesis.discriminator. "Third host" refers to Drew Afualo (C68).
claims.alternative: Comic register and Midwestern modesty weaken the discriminator; see type_hypothesis.against.

claims.claim: Asked about fear of failure, she said it isn't necessarily that; she describes fear of trying and of success.
claims.passage: The fear she names is the second clue. A Three's dread is usually failing in public. Asked directly, Reiter said, "I don't know if it's necessarily a fear of failure." What she describes instead is the danger of trying fully, and of success itself.
claims.inference: Built on C84, C85.
claims.alternative: She hedges ("maybe it kind of is").

claims.claim: In 2024 she prayed in gratitude that making little indie films with her friends would be enough, and in February 2026 she declined credit for an idea that came from improvising with friends.
claims.passage: And when she pictures enough, it is small and shared. Driving to the airport in 2024 after finishing a film shoot in Baton Rouge, she said, she prayed: "I'm so grateful if this is all it ever is is just like making like little indie films with my friends." Asked about credit for an idea in February 2026, she said, "it wasn't really my idea it was all of our idea cuz we were improvising."
claims.inference: S19 00:50:42-00:51:08 (Whisper; consecutive lines joined); S38 0:29:24-0:29:29. Belonging to a trusted group is central to what she says she wants. The S47 "I just want to make a movie with my friends" line was not re-located at draft and is not printed.
claims.alternative: She also takes pride in specific credit ("I casted everybody perfectly", S32) and in being the lead (C09). Sharing credit is also good collaborative practice.

claims.claim: Limits of the case: the follower ladder fits both types, much of the record is comedy, and she uses audience reaction as a gauge.
claims.passage: The case has limits. The follower ladder fits both types, because a Six can keep climbing when no number ever feels safe ("It never feels real," she told Piso). Much of the record is comedy, where self-deprecation is the joke. And she does use the audience as a gauge. Of a live show she said, "I'm always trying to like make people break cuz I'm like I want I need to know."
claims.alternative: These are the stated weaknesses of the type argument.

claims.claim: As of September 17, 2026, her father said SNL was not allowing her to give media interviews; no post-casting interview was found by October 16, 2026.
claims.passage: Her father said in September 2026 that SNL was not letting her give interviews, and none had appeared by mid-October.
claims.inference: Three episodes in. Performance roles are not personality evidence; the interview restriction explains the gap in post-casting first-person material.
claims.alternative: Early-season screen time fluctuates; do not build the argument on it.
claims.review_trigger: Check for her first post-casting long-form interview (likely during the season or at the end of it) and for any critical assessment of her SNL work.

claims.claim: The open test: how she describes what got her through a hard SNL week once she can give interviews.
claims.passage: When she can describe a hard week there at length, will she credit the response (Three), or the castmates, preparation and someone in charge who got her through it (Six)?
claims.inference: Settle signal derived from the discriminator; mirrors research follow-up (2).
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: At her first long-form post-casting interview, check whether she credits reception (Type 3) or castmates, preparation and leadership (Type 6).

claims.claim: On the parody set she was the friend insisting everyone take scenes seriously.
claims.passage: On the parody set, she told Yvette, she was "the one friend that's like no but like we have to take this serious you guys,"
claims.inference: S33 0:40:18-0:40:21 (December 3, 2025). Supports the Type 1 reading. The S33 "rule followery" and "we have to follow the rules" turns (shared with the host, medium attribution) are not printed.
claims.alternative: Type 1 would explain the enforcement of standards ("we have to take this serious", "we have to follow the rules. We have to be good", S33) and her self-labeling; Type 3 would explain driving the product. Directing a low-budget shoot with friends also simply requires someone to be in charge.

claims.claim: Against Type 1: her self-review concerns hurting people, is checked against others, and she describes a lifetime of half-effort.
claims.passage: But her self-review is about whether she hurt someone ("I said this like weird thing to my friend. What what how do I fix that now?"), she checks it against other people rather than an inner standard, and a One rarely describes a lifetime of half-effort.
claims.inference: S39 0:11:57-0:11:59 ("I said this like weird thing to my friend. What what how do I fix that now?"); C25.
claims.alternative: A One can also worry about wronging people.

claims.claim: Type 9 fits her self-described coasting, but she says she is most stressed when idle.
claims.passage: In 2022 she called herself "a procrastinator and a lazy person at heart," and she avoids confrontation. But a Nine settles when idle, and in 2024 she said "the most time when I get stressed is when I'm not doing stuff."
claims.inference: S18 00:17:54; S19 00:28:42 ("I think, I think the most time when I get stressed is when I'm not doing stuff"); confrontation avoidance from S33 (C22).
claims.alternative: Whisper transcripts; both statements are casual.

claims.claim: Her output (a weekly podcast for a year, a nearly 45-minute parody made with friends) contradicts the lazy label.
claims.passage: Her output, a weekly podcast for a year and a nearly 45-minute parody she produced with friends, also argues against the label.
claims.inference: Feed dates (S15); parody length (S09).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Leaving American High she asked friends to text her because she won't text first, not wanting to seem needy.
claims.passage: Leaving American High, she told friends, "please text me cuz like I won't text you," because "I don't want to feel like needy."
claims.inference: Sincere answers under questioning. Fear of seeming needy argues against a Type 2 reading. Ambivalence about closeness is compatible with Type 6 (trust takes time) and with a touring performer's life.
claims.alternative: Circumstance: frequent moves (Chippewa Falls, LA sublet, Eau Claire, Syracuse, New York) make "burst" friendships structural, as she says herself. Romantic history is private and should not be used as evidence.

claims.claim: After the Off-Broadway run of Ginger Twinsies (July to October 2025) she said she didn't know if she enjoyed the repetition but performing live every night was awesome, and that she needs novelty.
claims.passage: After _Ginger Twinsies_, an Off-Broadway parody of _The Parent Trap_ that ran from July to October 2025, she said, "I don't know if I enjoyed the repetition," but "performing live every night was awesome." Then: "I just need like novelty."
claims.inference: S46 0:34:33-0:34:42 (a host's "Right." interrupts after "repetition", so the quote is split) and 0:35:29. Run dates from S06/S09.
claims.alternative: Some coverage dates it as "last year" from 2026; use July-October 2025.

claims.claim: She keeps a couple of projects going so there is always something else to move on to.
claims.passage: She keeps "a couple projects going on at a time" so there is always "something else to immediately move on to."
claims.inference: A real feature of her working style that the Type 6 reading does not explain well; Type 7 and Type 3 explain it better. It may also be a way of managing anxiety about any single project's reception (she says moving on keeps her from getting "too caught up in the numbers", S22).
claims.alternative: Type 7 was tested and set aside because she reports not letting herself enjoy things (C31), guilt and dread rather than optimism, and fear rather than escape as the driver.

claims.claim: After a Harry Styles fan-fiction parody brought her about a million followers around 2020, she declined to keep making them.
claims.passage: When a parody of Harry Styles fan fiction brought her about a million followers around 2020, fans wanted more. "I'm not going to be like the Harry Styles girl," she decided. Five years later she put it more bluntly:
claims.inference: S22 0:51:20-0:52:02 ("it was the Harry Styles fanfiction that got me to like a million followers"; "I'm not going to be like the Harry Styles girl"). A costly choice against audience demand.
claims.alternative: Told comically; the regret is also comic ("I should have just kept making Harry Styles fanfiction"). Boredom (C36) may explain it as well as principle.

claims.claim: She later summarized the decision bluntly.
claims.passage: "Because the people wanted me to do it. And I said, 'Fuck the people.'"
claims.inference: S22 1:09:01-1:09:05, told comically; she also half-regrets it in jest elsewhere (S36).
claims.alternative: Boredom may explain it as well as principle.

claims.claim: She calls herself "not a risk taker" who is "protecting myself" (on four-wheelers, March 2025), yet a fellow comedian says she has no shame in pushing a joke.
claims.passage: She said in 2025 that she was "not a risk taker" and was "protecting myself" on a four-wheeler, yet Sedeño told her, "you have no shame to just like make the joke as hard as you can." A Six can push straight at what scares her, but the simpler reading may be that her risks happen inside a bit, where a character takes the hit.
claims.inference: S21 0:38:15-0:38:42; S36 0:15:14-0:15:26. The refused-kiss story (S40) is not used, per the sensitivity task.
claims.alternative: Counterevidence: her comedy takes social risks (gross-out videos, an oversharing podcast, a 45-minute parody), and she moved cities for work. The mix of caution and bold content fits a Type 6 phobic/counterphobic oscillation but also fits a performer whose risks are taken only inside a role. The kiss story is romantic and sensitive; use at most in her words, briefly.

claims.claim: She says she would shut down a riff she doesn't like, then calls that unfair.
claims.passage: She can be bossy, and she knows it. Telling the comedian Sabrina Wu on [_That's Enough_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2T-yIeGPqXs) in January 2026 how she handles riffs she doesn't like, she said, "I would shut that down immediately," and then judged herself: "And that's not fair."
claims.inference: S37 0:07:46-0:08:21 (January 12, 2026). The "have I given you a complex" question (medium attribution) is not printed.
claims.alternative: Directing collaborators also simply requires firmness.

claims.claim: Her younger sister, Molly, says it was hard to go on vacations with her for a while.
claims.passage: Her younger sister, Molly, says that for a while "it was really hard to go on vacations with you."
claims.inference: S32 0:27:31-0:27:34, after Grace calls her younger self hard to be around (a censored word; not quoted). Affectionate sibling teasing.
claims.alternative: Teasing on a comedy podcast; their parents are private and are not named in the article.

claims.claim: Her producer says she takes people at their word and is "so earnestly here."
claims.passage: Her producer, Lizzy Stewart, told her in the March 2026 anniversary episode, "if I tell you something you're going to assume that I'm telling you the truth," and "You're so earnestly here."
claims.inference: Independent testimony from close collaborators across 2025-2026 about trustingness and seriousness. Taking people at their word is notable for a Type 6 reading because it shows trust once given, not universal suspicion.
claims.alternative: Supports Types 1 and 6 about equally; "earnest" is also how her comedy is marketed (Rolling Stone, S12).

claims.claim: Her trust sits beside her worry that friends may not really be her friends.
claims.passage: That trust sits right beside her worry that her friends may not really be her friends.
claims.inference: Juxtaposes C35 and C71.
claims.alternative: Unresolved contradiction, left visible.

claims.claim: Her oversharing is selective: she says "the real overshare stuff would be like sad and like not funny," "nobody knows me and nobody knows actually really what I'm feeling," and "I don't want to tell these people all this stuff. That's why I have default to [gross-out humor]"; her producer says she has only ever asked for one cut, made to protect another person.
claims.passage: She told Soresi in 2025 that "the real overshare stuff would be like sad and like not funny." In October 2025, on [_Literally Life Changing_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2zVjVhc2TBY), she said "nobody knows me and nobody knows actually really what I'm feeling." Stewart says Reiter has only ever asked her to cut one story from the show: "You cut it for the other person."
claims.inference: S27 0:22:14 (September 15, 2025); S29 0:37:43 (October 22, 2025); S41 0:12:24-0:12:41 ("you've only ever asked me to cut one ... You cut it for the other person"). Gross-out persona as a shield; she guards others' privacy.
claims.alternative: Any type can keep private material private; this argues against reading her podcast as unfiltered self-revelation, not for a particular type. A Type 4 reading (feeling unknown) was tested and set aside: she withholds rather than cultivates the sadness and does not make difference or longing her subject.

claims.claim: A conversation recorded before the SNL casting and released September 23, 2026 included her repeating praise about herself.
claims.passage: recorded before the casting news and released on September 23, 2026, a week after it, Reiter repeated a line of praise about herself.
claims.inference: S47 1:27:48-1:28:01: the exchange ends with "I'm a light"; captions have no speaker names, so who first said the praise is not certain. The article says only that she repeated it.
claims.alternative: Speaker labels inferred from turn order.

claims.claim: Drew Afualo told her she was wincing when she said it but would come to believe it.
claims.passage: "You're you're you're wincing when you say it, but you will believe it."
claims.inference: S47 1:28:05-1:28:09; printed with the captioned repetitions. Third observer (after C17 and C64) of her discomfort with praise.
claims.alternative: Host encouragement on a self-confidence-themed show; part of a bit about learning from Drew.

claims.claim: Afualo added that if she keeps saying it, she will stop grimacing.
claims.passage: Keep saying it, Afualo added, and "you'll stop grimacing when you say it."
claims.inference: S47 1:28:11-1:28:14: "You keep saying it enough, you'll stop you'll stop grimacing when you say it." Only the words after the caption repetition are quoted.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Closing prediction: a Three would learn to believe the applause; a Six would keep wanting to hand it to someone else.
claims.passage: The two readings make different predictions from here. If Reiter is a Three, a season of applause will teach her to believe it. If she is a Six, the applause will keep feeling like something to hand to someone else.
claims.inference: Restates the discriminator as a forward test.
claims.alternative: An adult whose fame grows may simply habituate, whatever her type.
claims.review_trigger: Reassess at the next refresh using her post-SNL interviews.

claims.claim: Type FAQ mirrors the type answer at medium confidence.
claims.passage: Grace Reiter's personality type is Enneagram Type 6, the Loyalist, read at medium confidence. Sixes sit in the head triad, whose core emotion is fear. type_hypothesis.against: (1) The Type 3 case is substantial: since 2022 she has described her goal as being an "Internet persona" and worried about keeping the persona people liked (C05); she measures herself by followers and views on a ladder that is "never... enough", went to the Mall of America to be recognized, and would be "really really embarrassed" under a million views (C30); she is "work mode all the time" and does not let herself enjoy results (C31); she made the parody partly to "be the lead in a movie" (C09); and she has said "I don't exist unless I mean funny" and "I guess I'm truly just a shell" (S25, S40; claim removed at draft, lines not printed). (2) The Type 1 case: a daily list of her mistakes for her therapist and "I'm just like the worst person in the world" (C28), "we have to follow the rules. We have to be good" and enforcing seriousness on set (C27), self-described rigidity and taking everything seriously (C35), and moral lines such as refusing to punch down. (3) Circumstance and incentives: self-deprecation is her stated comic method ("comedy 101... just shit on yourself"), Midwestern modesty explains deflecting compliments, and a 23-to-25-year-old whose career jumped from TikTok to HBO, Netflix and SNL in a year has ordinary reasons for impostor feelings and dread (C11, C12). Much of the record is a comedy podcast whose premise is oversharing, so sincerity must be judged line by line, and several key lines (C19, C24) are half-jokes. (4) The evidence for caution and fear sits beside real boldness: gross-out videos, refusing to keep making the content that first went viral (C37), moving cities for work, self-described bluntness, and directing friends firmly (C27). (5) Novelty-seeking and many simultaneous projects (C36) and her self-described "coasting" and procrastination (C25) are not central Type 6 features. (6) In an episode recorded after the parody's release she said she no longer felt the pull toward religion and simply didn't think about it: "this is my life and this is the things I want to do" (C41), so the guilt may be easing as she adjusts. (7) She enjoys some recognition openly: being called Katniss "was kind of always my dream" (C67), and she wants attention on her birthday without asking for it (C81).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 3 is the strongest rival because her ambition is explicit, long-running and metric-driven (C05, C30): an early dream of being an online persona, escalating follower goals, recognition-seeking, embarrassment at modest view counts, "work mode all the time" (C31), strategic release planning (C10), and statements that locate her existence in performing (S25, S40; claim removed at draft, lines not printed). On this reading the praise-deflection (C16-C18) is image management: a self-preserving Three who does not want to look vain, and the guilt is about appearing egotistical. What strains the Type 3 reading: she moves away from approval when it arrives, independently observed by a roommate and a host (C17); she wants an outside authority to carry her success (C16, C26); she predicts her own downfall at the moment of success (C19); she fears trying fully rather than fearing failure (C25) and works best when someone else imposes the obligation; and her characteristic worry is whether people are secretly against her or will be mean to her (C20), not whether she is succeeding. A Three's self-protection usually takes the form of more efficient striving and polished image, not refusing compliments, apologizing for them, and asking "Is that okay?" on her own show. Type 1 was tested: the inner-critic material (C28) is real, but her self-review is about whether she hurt or offended people, she relies on others' reassurance rather than an inner standard, and she describes half-effort and mess tolerance that a One would not accept (C25). Type 9 was tested: coasting, going along with managers' decisions, retreat into video games and comfort TV, and conflict avoidance fit (C22, C25), but she is too vigilant, self-critical and anxious when idle (C31) for Nine. Type 2 was tested: she calls herself a people pleaser (C21) and shares credit (C34), but she avoids seeming needy, does not text first, and shows no pattern of making herself needed (C29). Type 7 (novelty, many projects, C36) and Type 4 (feeling unknown, C33) were tested and set aside: she reports guilt, dread and not letting herself enjoy things rather than optimism, and she withholds rather than cultivates her sadness.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What she does when approval actually arrives. A Type 3 moves toward admiration, takes it in as confirmation, and converts it into the next goal; a Type 6 treats it as unsettling and potentially dangerous, looks for something trustworthy outside herself to hold it, and braces for the ground to give way. Across May 2025 to September 2026, in host, guest and private-household settings, she does the second: "I can't handle this... if I believed in God, I could give all of it to God" (C16), "I'm for you guys" and talent she is only "the manager of" (C18), compliments answered with "I'm sorry" and a "wince" (C17), and "something's going to happen and it is my own hand that brings down myself" after her biggest hit (C19). Two people with daily access (her roommate) or extended conversation (Drew Afualo) independently describe the aversion. A second, supporting discriminator is where she gets steadiness under pressure: from preparation, obligations set by others, trusted collaborators and a wished-for mentor or authority (C23, C25, C26, C34), and from checking whether people are still with her ("Is that okay?", "Do you guys think of me differently now?", C20), rather than from the audience's applause. Limits: the escalating-goals evidence (C30) does not discriminate, both types fit it; she does use the audience as a gauge of whether material works ("I'm always trying to like make people break cuz I'm like I want I need to know", S46, about a live show), which is ordinary for a comic but is the Type 3 side of the second discriminator; much of the record is comic; and the discriminator rests on a performer's statements in a 17-month window during sudden fame. Hence medium confidence and the full jury.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her novelty-seeking and preference for "one and done" projects (C36). The early and persistent dream of being an online persona, and her saying she does not exist unless funny (C05; S25, S40), which Type 3 explains more naturally. Her repeated self-description as lazy and coasting against a record of heavy output (C25). The firmness with which she directs and corrects friends, and her harsh self-labels, beside her fear of confrontation and of offending (C22, C27). Her taking people at their word (C35) beside her worry that friends are secretly mocking her (C20). Her bold, sometimes transgressive comic content beside her self-description as "not a risk taker" (C24, C37). In 2024 she said she did not know if she could handle SNL's workload and preferred one-off projects, then pursued SNL again in 2026 (C12).
